## What a feature is

A feature is high level. It is what a customer tells a friend the product does, in the words they would use: "work at a glance", "pick up where I left off", "know why a run stopped". It names an outcome and why it matters, and nothing about how the product delivers it.

Altitude is the test, and it applies to every sentence of the doc, not only to its title. "Work at a glance" is a feature. "You can see the tasks in a menu" is not: it is one way of delivering that feature, and a reader has to picture a screen to understand it. The same outcome could be delivered by a menu, a board, a summary line or a notification, and the feature is what all of those have in common. If a candidate names a list, an order, a row, a click, a menu, a panel, a surface or a depth, it is a UX pattern. A pattern belongs to a feature; it is never a feature. One feature is usually delivered through several patterns, and those are the UX layer's to name.

Anything the product *does* is below a feature. How it groups, orders, ranks, arranges, remembers a choice, notifies, reminds, keeps asking, badges, names things or lets the person pick between arrangements is behaviour, and behaviour is the UX layer's to decide. A product doc that says work is grouped by workflow, or that a question keeps asking until it is answered, has designed the UX in product's clothing. Say what the person can now do and why it matters, and stop there.

Check every candidate three ways: it could be a bullet on the marketing page; an end user would understand it without a screenshot; and it would still be true if every screen were redesigned. A candidate that fails any one is too low. Name the outcome it serves and write that instead. Then check every sentence under it the same way: if a UX designer could deliver the feature and still disagree with the sentence, the sentence is a pattern, and it goes.

The issue is usually written below feature altitude: it names a panel, a list, a sort, a badge. That is what an issue looks like and it is not what a feature looks like. Do not promote the issue's mechanisms into features and do not carry them into the docs: name the outcomes those mechanisms serve. The mechanisms are not lost. The issue itself goes down to every later phase, and UX reads it when it chooses patterns. The features are at the right altitude when a reader who had never seen the issue could not tell from the docs which mechanisms it asked for.

Scale is the other test. A whole product has a dozen or so features over its life. One issue usually serves one feature, sometimes two, and never one feature per mechanism it names. Two outcomes a customer would name as one are one feature. A feature is the smallest outcome a customer would still name on its own, and smallest is measured in outcomes, never in interface: the smallest thing a customer would still name, not the smallest thing a designer would draw. Where one needs another first, say so in `requires`. Where two are related but independent, say so in `related`.

Each feature answers, in the doc's headings:

1. Who is served, named the way they would describe themselves, and what they cannot do today.
2. What they can now do, as `As a [who], I can [outcome] so that [why it matters]`. The outcome is a capability, never a mechanism, and the text under this heading stays at that altitude: what they can do, never what the product does to deliver it.
3. Why it matters to them, in the terms they would use.
4. How success shows, as a metric that moves only if the outcome is delivered.
5. What it requires and what it is related to.
6. Where it departs from `docs/product/principles.md`, and why, in one line. Silence means it conforms.

## What to produce

`features`: one entry per feature, in dependency order, each `{ id, story, importance, metrics, requires, related, doc_path }`. `importance` is 0 to 1 and is value if shipped. `doc_path` is `docs/product/<id>.md`.

`feature_docs`: one complete doc per feature, on `docs/_templates/product-feature.md`, in the same order.

`doc_paths`: one path per feature, in the same order.

`questions`: what only a person can settle and the docs cannot. Each `{ name, header, question, description, options: [{ value, description }], default, custom: true, optional: true }`. The default is the reading you took, as one of the options. Five a person will answer beat fifteen they will skip. Ask about what you added that the issue did not ask for.

`standing_amendment`: only when `docs/product/principles.md` is wrong.

`responses`: nothing on a first pass.

## How a doc is written

A doc is a standalone source of truth. Someone who has never seen this run, this conversation, or any earlier draft reads it and knows what is true.

- **Only what is true.** Every sentence states a fact about the product, the design or the code. Nothing is hedged, argued or defended.
- **As little as achieves the goal.** Keep a detail only if a reader would otherwise build the wrong thing, pick the wrong pattern, or miss something they need. Cut everything else.
- **Headings carry the idea.** Every heading is a sentence that states its conclusion. Reading the headings alone gives the whole doc; the text under a heading holds only the detail a builder needs.
- **One concept per file.** One feature, one pattern, one component, one unit. A doc that describes two things is two docs.
- **Layers reference upward only.** Product names people, goals and what they can do. UX names patterns and product features. UI names components, patterns and features. Engineering names units, components, patterns and features. No layer names anything from a layer below it: a product doc never names a class, a file, a table, a column or a component.
- **Each layer writes at its own altitude.** Product describes outcomes: what a person can now do and why it matters, never how. A list, an order, a row, a click, a panel or a screen in a product doc is a defect. UX describes interactions: the steps, the states, what the person knows at each. It never describes visuals. UI describes visuals: hierarchy, copy, states drawn. It never describes code. Engineering describes code.
- **No questions.** A doc holds answers. What cannot be settled from the docs is asked of the person now, through `questions`, and the answer is written in as a plain statement.
- **No alternatives, unless the choice goes against the usual way.** A doc does not list what was considered. Where it departs from the normal way of doing things, it states the departure and the reason in one line.
- **No process.** A doc never mentions a draft, a pass, a revision, a critique, a finding, a conversation, an earlier version of itself, or anything "previously" said. Where a decision changed, the doc states the decision that holds.
- **Frontmatter is the record.** The fields the template declares carry the links between layers. They are complete and they resolve.

Write in plain sentences. No em-dashes, no parentheses, no rhetorical questions.

## The answers

{{.inputs.answers}}

One key per question you raised, by name. A key that is present is settled: write the answer into the doc as a plain statement of what the product does. A key that is absent means the person had no view: your default stands, written the same way.

Some keys may name questions you did not raise: the person allowed follow-up questions, and those were asked and answered on the way. Treat them the same way.

Re-emit `features`, `feature_docs` and `doc_paths` in full, with `questions` empty.

## The critique

{{.inputs.findings}}

This is revision {{.inputs.iteration}}. For each finding: fix it, or say in one line why it is wrong, or say that a person has to decide and raise it as a question.

`responses`: one entry per finding, in order: `{ severity, claim, target_id, disposition: fixed | rejected | blocked, note }`. `note` says what changed, or why the finding is wrong, or which question carries it.

Re-emit `features`, `feature_docs`, `doc_paths` and `questions` in full. The docs state what holds now and nothing about what changed.

inputs.returned_findings.description: What a later phase found wrong with this one. Absent on the way down.

outputs.features.description: In dependency order: a feature comes after everything it requires.
